body: Tuesday, March 04 2025 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto
Information available before 2025-03-04 00:00 UTC. Prices use completed prior sessions. Prepared retrospectively; later outcomes are excluded.

Macro Stance: Growth is cooling at the margin rather than breaking. The ISM manufacturing index printed 50.3 for February [1], and Reuters summed up the month as “US manufacturing stable, price pressures surge ahead of tariffs storm” [2]. The slowdown signals are real: The Hill reported the Atlanta Fed’s model pointing to negative 1.5 percent GDP growth in the first quarter [3], and fourth-quarter growth of 2.3% annualised only matched estimates [4]. Inflation is cooling on the data, with January PCE up 2.5% [5], and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sees inflation falling to the Fed’s 2% target despite the tariffs [6]. Reuters also reported that the Commerce Secretary wants government spending removed from the GDP tally [7], which would change how the growth number reads. Keep the macro call at neutral and let the next prints decide the direction.

Rates & Curve: Treasuries are rallying and the curve is bull flattening. At the prior close the US Treasury par curve had the 2Y at 3.96% and the 10Y at 4.16%, which puts the 10Y-2Y spread at +20 bps and the 10Y-3M spread at -19 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-03). Over 20 observations the 2Y fell 26 bps and the 10Y fell 42 bps, which left the spread 16 bps lower. The curve is positive but very flat, and the move is bull flattening, so the long end is doing most of the work. Equities are where the strain shows. The S&P 500 closed at 5,849.72, down 1.76% in the prior session and 3.16% over 20 sessions, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 4.90% over 20 sessions to 20,425.58 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). The VIX rose 16.05% in the prior session to 22.78, up 6.35 index points over 20 sessions, and the US Dollar Index slipped to 106.75 index points, down 1.49% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).

New / Most Important: The tariff start date is the event. Reuters reported that Trump locked in tariffs on Canada and Mexico to launch on Tuesday, and stocks tumbled [8]. AP quoted him saying there is “no room” for delay on the 25% levies [9]. China has announced counter-tariffs of up to 15% on some US goods from March 10 [10]. Options desks were positioning for the damage: MarketWatch reported traders bracing for a stock-market crash [11], and Bloomberg reported zero-day options trading hitting a record on the Trump turmoil and a Robinhood push [12].

Playbook ✓: Keep US equity exposure near neutral and buy protection rather than chasing the bounce. Own the cash-flow leaders and avoid adding Nasdaq 100 beta, which is down 4.90% over 20 sessions, until the VIX stops rising from 22.78. Hedge the tariff start with a small index put position or a VIX position sized to survive a sharp reversal. The call turns constructive if the S&P 500 reclaims its 6,040.53 close from 31 January while the 10Y stays near 4.16%. It turns defensive if the 10Y reverses the bull flattening and climbs back toward its 4.58% level from 31 January, because that would mean the rate rally has stopped sheltering equities.

Macro Stance: Europe has moved from austerity talk to a spending plan, and the market is paying for it. Macron urged Europe to lift defence spending above 3 percent of GDP [13], and Bloomberg reported European defence stocks jumping on the leaders’ military spending pledge [14]. Yahoo Finance UK wrote that European stocks closed at a record high, led by defence shares [15]. Reuters reported Germany eyeing swift moves on defence [16]. The index tape confirms the breadth: the STOXX Europe 600 closed at 563.13, up 1.07% in the prior session and 5.29% over 20 sessions, and the DAX gained 8.02% over 20 sessions to 23,147.02 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Rheinmetall rose 13.71% in the prior session to 1,144.50 EUR and is up 49.80% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).

Credit & Inflation: Inflation is diverging across the Atlantic, and that matters for the rate path. Reuters reported investors betting on the sharpest US–Europe inflation divergence since 2022 [17]. The ECB’s tone is split: a Reuters Morning Bid column says the bank may stumble into stimulus [18], while Schnabel says ECB rates are no longer a material drag on growth [19]. On credit, the Bundesbank chief warned that Germany’s economy is 5 minutes to midnight after the central bank’s first loss in 45 years [20], and S&P turned its outlook on France negative [21]. The spread between German and French sovereign paper is the gauge to watch as the defence borrowing takes shape.

New / Most Important: Germany is the pivot. Reuters reported Germany eyeing swift moves on defence [16], and Bloomberg reported Europe’s rearmament prompting traders to bet on the Swedish krona [22]. The signal is that the spending is becoming a currency story as well as an equity story, which makes the defence trade more than a sector bet.

Playbook ✓: Own the broad STOXX 600 and the German industrials that the spending plan touches, and treat the defence names as event trades. Rheinmetall is up 49.80% over 20 sessions, so the easy part of that move is done and new money should wait for a pullback. Avoid French sovereign-linked exposure until the budget picture clears, given the negative outlook [21]. The call turns defensive if a Ukraine truce takes hold and cuts the defence premium, or if the ECB confirms stimulus outright, which would weigh on the euro, now at 1.0414 and up 1.62% over 20 sessions.

Macro Stance: China is caught between a factory rebound and a tariff war. Reuters reported February manufacturing hitting a three-month high, while the US tariff war clouds the outlook [23]. China’s non-manufacturing PMI was 50.4 in February, according to China Daily [24]. Beijing is answering the new US levies rather than absorbing them. Reuters reported extra tariffs of 10% to 15% on various US farm products [25], and Bloomberg reported Beijing vowing “all necessary measures” against the new tariffs [26]. The stance is mixed: the factory data argue for stabilisation, and the tariff calendar argues for a fresh drag.

PMIs & Activity: Factories are the best-supported number. Reuters reported factory activity picking up, with trade uncertainties weighing [27], and the Guardian wrote that Chinese manufacturing returned to growth despite the threat of higher Trump tariffs [28]. The latest private PMI is January’s, when Caixin showed factory growth slowing [29], so February’s private reading is the number that would confirm or kill the recovery view. Consumers are weaker than factories. Hong Kong’s January retail sales value fell 3.2% [30], and SCMP asked why Chinese travellers are shunning the US and Europe [31].

Credit Impulse: The credit reading is the weakest link, so the view rests on policy direction rather than a fresh print. The most recent marker is from late February, when Reuters reported Chinese banks heeding a PBOC call to cut dollar deposit rates [32]. That is a push from the central bank, not evidence that borrowers are coming back. What would confirm the view is a loan figure in which household and corporate borrowing turns up for two months running. Until then, treat the factory rebound as a cyclical bounce rather than a credit upturn, and size China-linked positions to match.

Property: Prices are still falling, but more slowly. Reuters reported second-hand home price declines narrowing for a seventh straight month in February [33], while a Reuters poll expects home prices to drop further [34]. More distress is expected in Hong Kong property, where Winland is divesting assets [35], and hedge funds have started betting on a turnaround in the unloved sector [36]. A further month of narrowing declines would support the turnaround bets; a renewed fall in second-hand prices would undercut them.

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Trade is the policy story, and it runs in both directions. Trump said the US will impose an additional 10% tariff on China [37]. China retaliated against US farm products [38], and CNBC reported counter-tariffs of up to 15% on some US goods from March 10 [10]. Domestic policy is opening rather than closing: China opened its telecoms sector to 13 foreign companies [39], and the Guardian reported the Two Sessions opening in Beijing as the world order roils [40]. A large new stimulus package is not the base case, so treat fiscal support as an option rather than a forecast.

Markets & Flows: Hong Kong is the strongest tape. The Hang Seng closed at 23,006.27, up 13.80% over 20 sessions though down 1.44% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). The mainland is lagging. The Shanghai Composite closed at 3,316.93 index points, up 1.98% over 20 sessions and down 1.66% over five. The CSI 300 tracker ASHR closed at 26.39 USD, down 0.68% in the prior session. KWEB, the China internet ETF, closed at 33.34 USD, up 6.59% over 20 sessions. The dollar-yuan rate rose 1.35% over 20 sessions to 7.2828, a weaker yuan (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Listings are drawing demand: Reuters reported Mixue jumping 47% on its Hong Kong debut as IPO volumes rebounded [41], and SCMP reported Chinese consumer stocks in demand as Mixue rides the IPO revival [42].

New / Most Important: Advanced chips are still reaching China. The Wall Street Journal reported Chinese buyers ordering Nvidia’s newest AI chips in defiance of US curbs [43], and Nikkei Asia reported Singapore suspecting Nvidia chips were smuggled via Malaysia [44]. This is the signal that matters because it ties the tech cycle to the export-control story, and both to the Hong Kong rally pulling the index higher. The consumer-tech side of the same story is visible too: Yahoo Finance reported Tencent’s AI bot passing DeepSeek as China’s favourite on iPhones [45].

Playbook ✓: Own Hong Kong internet and consumer names on confirmation. KWEB and the Hang Seng are the cleanest exposure, but buy them on pullbacks rather than chasing a 13.80% run over 20 sessions. Trim onshore A-share beta through ASHR if the counter-tariffs of March 10 [10] start to bite, and hedge the yuan leg, since dollar-yuan is up 1.35% over 20 sessions. The call changes if the official factory reading holds at a three-month high while loan data stay weak, because that combination means the rebound is an inventory story. ⚠ Divergence: the Hang Seng is up 13.80% over 20 sessions while Hong Kong’s January retail sales value fell 3.2% [30], so the market is pricing a consumer recovery the spending data have not yet shown.

Macro Stance: Japan is absorbing the tariff shock through its corporate spending. Reuters reported Japanese corporate capex dropping for the first time in four years amid tariff fears [46], and the Bank of Japan chief warned of strong global uncertainty due to US tariffs [47]. Traders placed a record bet on a rising yen and further rate hikes [48]. The Japan Times wrote that Japanese stocks have stalled at 1989 levels as investors weigh tariffs and rates [49]. The macro read is weak demand with a firm currency, which is a poor mix for equities.

Activity & Currency: The yen is doing the work. USD/JPY closed at 150.7710, up 0.51% in the prior session but down 2.96% over 20 sessions, while the Nikkei 225 closed at 37,785.47, up 1.70% in the prior session and down 4.37% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Exporters carry the currency risk. Tokyo Electron fell 11.75% over 20 sessions to 22,380.00 JPY and Advantest fell 7.55% to 8,128.00 JPY, while Toyota rose 3.94% in the prior session to 2,795.00 JPY (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Households feel the cost side as well: The Japan Times reported consumers hunting for bargains as food inflation bites [50].

Playbook ✓: Stay underweight unhedged Japanese equities into the tariff start, and keep the yen as the funding-currency hedge that protects the book. Buy exporters only once the yen weakens. The trigger is USD/JPY back toward 155.3630, its 3 February level, which would restore the export tailwind. Until then, prefer domestic cyclicals with pricing power, and avoid adding to the semiconductor-equipment names that have fallen 11.75% and 7.55% over 20 sessions. The call changes if the Nikkei reclaims its 39,513.97 reference from 30 January with the yen still firm.

Macro Stance: A rate cut has ended the housing downturn. Reuters reported Australia’s housing market ending its downturn as the rate cut lifted sentiment [51]. The Reserve Bank’s own warning is the counterweight: weak incomes and high inflation if productivity lags [52]. AFR’s headline put it bluntly, that Chalmers has “damaged” RBA independence [53], which keeps the policy outlook noisy. The rate-cut tailwind is real but narrow, and the demand side is not yet strong enough to carry the equity market.

Demand & Financing: The Australian dollar closed at 0.6221 and the ASX 200 at 8,245.70 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). AUD/USD is down 2.35% over five sessions, while the index is down 1.60% over 20. Iron ore is the pressure point: it logged a monthly loss on China steel export concerns [54]. Financing is migrating: AFR reported global private credit funds set to storm Australia [55], and the banks are fighting over mortgage brokers, with CBA and NAB grappling with the rise of the broker channel [56]. BHP rose 1.43% in the prior session to 39.60 AUD.

Playbook ✓: Stay neutral on the ASX 200 and favour the banks only with a view on mortgage pricing. Keep iron-ore producers as a tactical trade rather than a core holding until China’s steel exports stabilise. The call turns constructive if AUD/USD reclaims its 0.6144 level from 3 February with the index holding its 8,379.40 reference from the same date. It turns defensive if the rate-cut sentiment fades and the housing rebound stalls.

Macro Stance: Poland is the one European market with a domestic turn. Bloomberg reported the zloty surging to a 10-year high against the dollar, fanned by a hawkish central bank [57]. A Polish manufacturing PMI signals a revival in industry and an end to almost three years of recession [58]. Wages keep rising: GUS published 2024 wage data showing Poles earning more [59]. Housing prices are rising more slowly than inflation, and developers are holding their per-square-metre prices [60]. Bankier reported the euro back up to 4.20 zloty [61], and Santander Bank warned that a strong zloty could weigh on GDP [62]. The zloty is strong, but the currency gain is not free: Business Insider Polska warned that a strong zloty is not only a benefit [63].

Markets: Poland’s proxies are up strongly. EPOL closed at 25.68 USD, up 8.68% over 20 sessions, and the WIG20TR tracker closed at 49.42 PLN, up 8.68% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). USD/PLN closed at 4.0048, down 2.73% over 20 sessions, and EUR/PLN at 4.1701, down 1.16%. Leadership is rotating toward energy and banks, and the spread is wide: Orlen closed at 64.12 PLN, up 21.05% over 20 sessions, against Allegro’s decline over the same window; mBank at 743.80 PLN, up 18.82%; PZU at 54.86 PLN, up 10.43%; and PKO Bank Polski at 69.92 PLN, up 6.33%. Consumer names are strong too: LPP at 18,210.00 PLN is up 13.67% and Dino Polska at 500.00 PLN is up 11.41%, while Allegro, at 28.09 PLN, is down 1.92% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Smaller names are moving too: JSW rose 12.03% over 20 sessions to 25.70 PLN, Asseco Poland rose 20.76% to 139.60 PLN, and CD Projekt rose 5.84% to 221.00 PLN (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Foreign money is in the bonds: Bankier reported more than ten central banks holding Polish treasuries [64], and Money.pl reported foreign central banks buying Polish treasuries as “big, strong players” [65].

Fiscal & Politics: The budget is the policy weak spot. Balcerowicz criticised spending that makes no sense under the current government [66]. The presidential race is tightening: POLITICO reported the nationalists sticking to Trump like glue ahead of the election [67], and an opinion poll suggests the pro-Kremlin candidate could enter the second round [68]. The president has vowed to spend 4.7% of GDP on defence this year [69], which is the fiscal anchor for the defence stocks. Governance is in the headlines as well: media reported a former Orlen board member detained by the CBA anti-corruption bureau [70], a story that sits awkwardly beside the dividend narrative.

Corporate & Sectors: Orlen is the anchor. Orlen and Equinor agreed to develop carbon capture projects [71], and Strefa Inwestorów reported that Orlen’s 2025 dividend could be the highest in its history [72]. Bank Pekao earned 6.4 billion zloty and wants to pay out half of it in dividends [73]. Dino is growing in a weak market and set a new all-time high [74]. Defence is the hottest theme in European equities, with shares setting fresh records [75]. Mining is less comfortable: a series of strong tremors hit two KGHM mines [76]. PGE GiEK’s chief says the Bełchatów site has all the advantages for a second nuclear plant [77]. PZU named Andrzej Klesyk as its new chief executive to lead Poland’s largest insurer [78].

Geopolitics & Security: The security backdrop is active. Poland scrambled military aircraft as Russian missiles targeted western Ukraine [79]. A report found Russia paid operatives to paint anti-government graffiti in Poland [80]. The Polish space agency is investigating a cyberattack on its systems [81], and Wałęsa said Trump’s treatment of Zelenskyy filled him with horror [82]. Polish equities trade the war as well: Ukrainian stocks surged on the Warsaw exchange on talk of a peace plan [83].

New / Most Important: The one signal that matters is the manufacturing turn meeting a strong currency. A PMI that signals revival [58], with the zloty at a 10-year high against the dollar [57], is the combination that lifts banks and domestic cyclicals while squeezing exporters.

Playbook ✓: Own the banks (PKO, Pekao, mBank) and Orlen on dividend visibility, and keep the defence names as a smaller satellite because their 20-session moves are extreme. Hedge the zloty leg with a modest EUR/PLN position, since a strong currency hurts exporters, and keep that hedge small so a currency reversal does not swamp the equity gain. The WIG20TR tracker at 49.42 PLN is the level to hold; a close back below its 45.47 PLN reference from 3 February would reopen the risk. ⚠ Divergence: a zloty at a 10-year high [57] against a manufacturing revival means exporters priced for a weak currency will lag the banks.

Narrative: The consensus still treats AI spending as the engine, but the leaders have turned. The technology ETF closed at 218.67 USD, down 3.04% in the prior session and 5.26% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Nvidia shares fell 9% on tariff fears, CNBC reported [84], and Forbes put it as Nvidia tanking as tariffs sink stocks [85]. Nvidia closed at 114.06 USD, down 8.69% in the prior session and 5.01% over 20 sessions from 120.07 USD on 31 January. The driver that matters now is the tariff overhang on the hardware cycle, not the demand story.

Reported: Dell reported a full-year EPS beat [86] and then lifted its dividend 18% alongside a $10 billion buyback [87]. Snowflake posted a big beat and the stock jumped, Barron’s reported [88]. Pure Storage beat on Q4 yet fell 12% in premarket trade, which Stocktwits framed as retail scrambling to buy the dip [89].

EPS Upside Watch: The set-up is in the hardware names that have been cut hardest. Nvidia’s guidance was optimistic but did not convince Wall Street [90], so the next print has to clear a bar the market already doubts. Dell’s buyback signals management confidence in cash generation, which makes its EPS path the cleaner set-up at 95.56 USD, down 7.76% over 20 sessions.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Beats are being sold. Pure Storage beat and still slid [89], and Nvidia’s 78% sales growth [91] did not stop the stock falling. Nvidia and Broadcom are testing chips on Intel’s manufacturing process, Reuters reported [92], a story about share moving between foundries rather than the AI pie growing.

Narrative: Platforms are split between advertising and AI optionality. The communication services ETF closed at 100.98 USD, down 1.00% in the prior session and 1.37% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Yahoo Finance laid out two reasons Meta broke its winning streak [93], while CNBC reported Meta planning a standalone AI app to compete with ChatGPT [94]. Alphabet fell 18.14% over 20 sessions to 167.01 USD.

Reported: Alphabet’s cost cuts are the most concrete corporate event in the sector: Google announced layoffs in its HR and cloud units as part of ongoing cost cuts [95]. Meta’s streak break is a share move rather than a reported result, so the sector’s reported side is thin and the narrative does the work.

EPS Upside Watch: Meta is set up on relative value, not on earnings. It closed at 655.05 USD, down 4.95% over 20 sessions, after the streak break [93]. The upside case is that the AI app adds engagement without adding cost, which is the question the next print has to answer. Netflix, at 973.70 USD and down 0.31% over 20 sessions, is the quieter defensive alternative.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The ad giants are no longer moving together. Alphabet is down 18.14% over 20 sessions while Meta is down 4.95%, so the sector is being sorted by company rather than traded as a block (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).

Narrative: Banks are being sold on the curve and on the tariff backdrop. The financials ETF closed at 51.74 USD, down 0.84% in the prior session but up 0.52% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Goldman Sachs warned that the S&P 500 rally may falter after a 5% selloff [96]. Goldman closed at 605.26 USD, down 5.49% over 20 sessions, and JPMorgan at 260.62 USD, down 2.50%.

Reported: BNY Mellon’s full-year 2024 revenue beat with EPS in line [97], and Goldman Sachs’ full-year 2024 results beat expectations [98]. The weak print was Ready Capital, whose shares plunged 28% after a Q4 loss and a dividend cut [99]. State Street agreed to buy Mizuho’s global custody business [100], a fee-franchise move rather than a balance-sheet one.

EPS Upside Watch: The upside is in custody and fee franchises, not in loan books. Regional lenders are the laggards: the regional-bank ETF KRE is down 4.64% over 20 sessions, so the sector needs evidence that funding costs are easing before the regional EPS lift is credible.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The big banks beat and still traded lower. BNY beat on revenue and Goldman beat [97] [98], yet Goldman is down 5.49% and Morgan Stanley down 6.72% over 20 sessions, so the sector is being priced on rates and tariffs rather than on the reported numbers.

Narrative: Oil is falling while gas is spiking. WTI closed at 68.37 USD, down 5.74% over 20 sessions, and Brent at 71.62 USD, down 6.70% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). The energy ETF closed at 87.82 USD, down 3.49% in the prior session. Henry Hub gas rose 35.41% over 20 sessions to 4.12 USD per MMBtu, and Reuters reported US natgas prices jumping 8% on record LNG flows [101].

Reported: The energy reporting in the window is thin, and the hard data point is gas. Reuters reported the jump on record LNG flows [101], and in the same news cycle Germany was reported not to be in talks to revive the Nord Stream 2 pipeline [102], which keeps the pipeline route closed for now.

EPS Upside Watch: The set-up is gas, not crude. Producers with gas exposure are the names that gain if the LNG flows hold. Exxon closed at 107.76 USD, up 0.87% over 20 sessions, and Chevron at 153.09 USD, up 2.61%, while ConocoPhillips, at 92.63 USD, is down 6.27% and is the most crude-exposed of the three.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The usual oil-and-gas pairing has broken. Gas is up 35.41% over 20 sessions while crude is down 5.74%, and the energy ETF is only up 0.21% over the same window, which says the market is not paying for the gas move in the majors (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).

Narrative: Factories are holding while the tariffs threaten the supply chain. The ISM manufacturing index printed 50.3 for February [1], but TradingView reported the slowdown coming in more than expected [103], and price pressures surged ahead of the tariffs [2]. The industrials ETF closed at 134.39 USD, down 1.42% in the prior session and 2.86% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).

Reported: Rolls-Royce upgraded its forecasts and its shares soared more than 18%, Investing.com reported [104]. The Caterpillar line is weaker: it is down 10.61% over 20 sessions to 332.04 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).

EPS Upside Watch: Rolls-Royce has shown the template: a guidance upgrade is rewarded even in a soft industrial tape. The next industrials with a cash-flow guide are the set-up. Airbus, at 174.38 EUR, rose 5.24% in the prior session and 4.68% over 20 sessions, so the European aerospace leg has momentum going into any print.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The manufacturing data are holding up better than the stock tape. An ISM reading of 50.3 [1] sits beside an ETF down 2.86% over 20 sessions, which says the market is discounting tariffs, not the current factory activity.

Narrative: Consumer discretionary is where the damage shows. The sector ETF closed at 211.98 USD, down 1.84% in the prior session and 8.70% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Tesla is the largest single reason. Morgan Stanley reinstated it as a top pick with a $430 target [105], but the stock is down 29.65% over 20 sessions. Target fell 12.44% over 20 sessions to 120.76 USD, and Lululemon fell 16.03% to 347.81 USD.

Reported: Tesla sales almost halved in Europe last month and were surpassed by a Chinese rival, Business Insider reported [106]. Reuters reported Tesla’s market value tumbling below $1 trillion as its Europe sales slumped [107]. Those are the reported facts the bulls have to argue around.

EPS Upside Watch: The next consumer print is the test, and the bar is low. Target and Lululemon have already been cut hard over 20 sessions, so a guidance hold would be enough to lift the group. Warren Buffett said tariffs leave consumers footing the bill [108], which keeps the discretionary bar high on pricing.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The habit this cuts against is buying the Tesla dip. Musk’s claim that Tesla’s profit could grow tenfold over five years [109] runs against a sales slump in the cars that define the sector.

Narrative: Staples are quietly working. The staples ETF closed at 83.52 USD, up 0.53% in the prior session and 5.75% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Coca-Cola rose 13.93% over 20 sessions to 72.32 USD, and Costco rose 6.83% to 1,046.85 USD. The defensive bid is real, and it is not a sign of a consumer boom.

Reported: Kroger, a Buffett pick, paid investors, 24/7 Wall St. reported [110]. The concrete corporate news is pricing: Walmart rose 4.18% over five sessions to 97.59 USD, and Procter & Gamble rose 5.78% over 20 sessions to 175.59 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).

EPS Upside Watch: Pricing power is the upside case. Staples can hold margins if they pass tariff costs on, but Buffett’s point that consumers pay the tariff bill [108] puts a limit on how far that goes. Walmart and Costco are the names with the strongest set-up on that test.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Staples rise while discretionary falls, which is the defensive rotation in plain sight. The convention that a risk-off tape lifts only gold and utilities is breaking, because the staples are doing the work (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).

Narrative: Health care is the defensive with a story. The sector ETF closed at 149.58 USD, up 1.85% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Eli Lilly rose 14.63% over 20 sessions to 929.72 USD, and Bank of America raised its Madrigal target to $239 from $154 [111]. The sector is being bought for growth as well as for safety.

Reported: Hims & Hers plunged 22% on concerns over its weight-loss business and margins [112], and Reuters reported looming curbs on drug compounding clouding the forecast [113]. Hims & Hers’ full-year 2024 results came in line with expectations [114].

EPS Upside Watch: Lilly is the momentum name, and its upside is in the next print rather than the price. Madrigal’s target raise [111] is the analyst set-up, with the upside resting on the next print rather than on the stock’s recent move.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The managed-care half of health care is not working. UnitedHealth is down 13.91% over 20 sessions to 467.05 USD while the sector ETF is up 1.85%, so the sector average hides a split between drug names and insurers.

Narrative: Materials are split between copper and steel. The materials ETF closed at 86.98 USD, down 2.01% in the prior session and 2.04% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Iron ore logged a monthly loss on China steel export concerns [54]. Copper is the asset here, not a China growth gauge: it closed at 4.58 USD per pound, up 7.38% over 20 sessions, on the AI data-centre and grid build-out.
Reported: Freeport-McMoRan closed at 35.53 USD, down 0.89% over 20 sessions, and Alcoa at 31.33 USD, down 11.30%. Money.pl argued that Europe must invest in mining to build a copper future [115].

EPS Upside Watch: Copper miners are the set-up, and their earnings upside rides the metal. Freeport’s 35.53 USD close is the level that matters, since it has barely moved while copper has risen 7.38% over 20 sessions.

Historical Analog: The closest analog is a mechanism rather than a dated episode, and it runs in two waves. First come the early call buyers: their options force the dealers who sold them to buy stock as a hedge, and that hedging pushes the price higher. Second comes the crowd, which buys the same options after the move is already visible, so the squeeze depends on late buyers continuing to arrive. A crash bet runs the same loop in reverse. Dealers who sold puts sell stock as the market falls, and the crowd buys protection after the first leg down. Retail is in the second wave for the same reason: the contract is easy to buy after a visible drop, while the first wave of hedgers is already positioned.

CNBC reported it tumbling 9% and reversing most of the rally from the announcement [142], and it closed at 86,065.67 USD, down 10.11% over 20 sessions from 95,747.43 on 11 February (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). The flow is the warning: a record $2.9 billion left crypto funds [147]. The instrument risk is timing: one trader made millions betting $200 million on bitcoin just before the reserve news [144], and buyers who arrive after the headline carry the reverse risk.

Why Retail Is Here: The pitch is that AI needs more power than the grid can supply, and small modular reactors are the clean way to supply it. Palisades’ agreement to build the first of its kind small modular reactors in Michigan made the case [137], and Reuters reported Siemens Energy supplying equipment for Rolls-Royce’s small reactors [136]. The trade has a skeptic, though. Seeking Alpha’s note on NuScale is titled ‘Sell’, arguing that small modular reactors are unestablished and costly [182]. NuScale closed at 15.45 USD, down 10.12% in the session and 35.19% over 20 sessions from 23.84 on 31 January (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).

Where It Breaks: The break is the rotation. WSJ reported on 1 March that AI fever in power stocks had moved from nuclear to plain natural gas [183], and Jim Cramer said he was ‘very, very skeptical’ of nuclear power trades [184]. NuScale published its fourth-quarter and full-year results on 3 March [185], and the stock fell 16.31% over five sessions, so the market is waiting for proof that the reactor case pays. Oklo and Nano Nuclear are down 29.39% and 29.57% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03), so the group moves together, and a 10% session shows how little cushion a single name has.

Growth is cooling at the margin rather than breaking. The ISM manufacturing index printed 50.3 for February [[n8278]], and Reuters summed up the month as “US manufacturing stable, price pressures surge ahead of tariffs storm” [[n1315]]. The slowdown signals are real: The Hill reported the Atlanta Fed’s model pointing to negative 1.5 percent GDP growth in the first quarter [[n8526]], and fourth-quarter growth of 2.3% annualised only matched estimates [[n8151]]. Inflation is cooling on the data, with January PCE up 2.5% [[n8207]], and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sees inflation falling to the Fed’s 2% target despite the tariffs [[n8656]]. Reuters also reported that the Commerce Secretary wants government spending removed from the GDP tally [[n8248]], which would change how the growth number reads. Keep the macro call at neutral and let the next prints decide the direction.
Rates & Curve

Treasuries are rallying and the curve is bull flattening. At the prior close the US Treasury par curve had the 2Y at 3.96% and the 10Y at 4.16%, which puts the 10Y-2Y spread at +20 bps and the 10Y-3M spread at -19 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-03). Over 20 observations the 2Y fell 26 bps and the 10Y fell 42 bps, which left the spread 16 bps lower. The curve is positive but very flat, and the move is bull flattening, so the long end is doing most of the work. Equities are where the strain shows. The S&P 500 closed at 5,849.72, down 1.76% in the prior session and 3.16% over 20 sessions, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 4.90% over 20 sessions to 20,425.58 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). The VIX rose 16.05% in the prior session to 22.78, up 6.35 index points over 20 sessions, and the US Dollar Index slipped to 106.75 index points, down 1.49% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).
New / Most Important

The tariff start date is the event. Reuters reported that Trump locked in tariffs on Canada and Mexico to launch on Tuesday, and stocks tumbled [[n3926]]. AP quoted him saying there is “no room” for delay on the 25% levies [[n3928]]. China has announced counter-tariffs of up to 15% on some US goods from March 10 [[n1259]]. Options desks were positioning for the damage: MarketWatch reported traders bracing for a stock-market crash [[n5377]], and Bloomberg reported zero-day options trading hitting a record on the Trump turmoil and a Robinhood push [[n5412]].
Playbook ✓

Keep US equity exposure near neutral and buy protection rather than chasing the bounce. Own the cash-flow leaders and avoid adding Nasdaq 100 beta, which is down 4.90% over 20 sessions, until the VIX stops rising from 22.78. Hedge the tariff start with a small index put position or a VIX position sized to survive a sharp reversal. The call turns constructive if the S&P 500 reclaims its 6,040.53 close from 31 January while the 10Y stays near 4.16%. It turns defensive if the 10Y reverses the bull flattening and climbs back toward its 4.58% level from 31 January, because that would mean the rate rally has stopped sheltering equities.

Macron urged Europe to lift defence spending above 3 percent of GDP [[n2934]], and Bloomberg reported European defence stocks jumping on the leaders’ military spending pledge [[n2918]]. Yahoo Finance UK wrote that European stocks closed at a record high, led by defence shares [[n2920]]. Reuters reported Germany eyeing swift moves on defence [[n5359]]. Credit & Inflation

Inflation is diverging across the Atlantic, and that matters for the rate path. Reuters reported investors betting on the sharpest US–Europe inflation divergence since 2022 [[n2827]]. The ECB’s tone is split: a Reuters Morning Bid column says the bank may stumble into stimulus [[n2910]], while Schnabel says ECB rates are no longer a material drag on growth [[n2779]]. On credit, the Bundesbank chief warned that Germany’s economy is 5 minutes to midnight after the central bank’s first loss in 45 years [[n2828]], and S&P turned its outlook on France negative [[n2882]]. The spread between German and French sovereign paper is the gauge to watch as the defence borrowing takes shape.
New / Most Important

Germany is the pivot. Reuters reported Germany eyeing swift moves on defence [[n5359]], and Bloomberg reported Europe’s rearmament prompting traders to bet on the Swedish krona [[n2921]]. The signal is that the spending is becoming a currency story as well as an equity story, which makes the defence trade more than a sector bet.
Playbook ✓

Own the broad STOXX 600 and the German industrials that the spending plan touches, and treat the defence names as event trades. Rheinmetall is up 49.80% over 20 sessions, so the easy part of that move is done and new money should wait for a pullback. Avoid French sovereign-linked exposure until the budget picture clears, given the negative outlook [[n2882]]. The call turns defensive if a Ukraine truce takes hold and cuts the defence premium, or if the ECB confirms stimulus outright, which would weigh on the euro, now at 1.0414 and up 1.62% over 20 sessions.

China is caught between a factory rebound and a tariff war. Reuters reported February manufacturing hitting a three-month high, while the US tariff war clouds the outlook [[n1220]]. China’s non-manufacturing PMI was 50.4 in February, according to China Daily [[n1193]]. Beijing is answering the new US levies rather than absorbing them. Reuters reported extra tariffs of 10% to 15% on various US farm products [[n1260]], and Bloomberg reported Beijing vowing “all necessary measures” against the new tariffs [[n1022]]. The stance is mixed: the factory data argue for stabilisation, and the tariff calendar argues for a fresh drag.
PMIs & Activity

Factories are the best-supported number. Reuters reported factory activity picking up, with trade uncertainties weighing [[n1224]], and the Guardian wrote that Chinese manufacturing returned to growth despite the threat of higher Trump tariffs [[n1228]]. The latest private PMI is January’s, when Caixin showed factory growth slowing [[n0449]], so February’s private reading is the number that would confirm or kill the recovery view. Consumers are weaker than factories. Hong Kong’s January retail sales value fell 3.2% [[n1276]], and SCMP asked why Chinese travellers are shunning the US and Europe [[n1320]].
Credit Impulse

The credit reading is the weakest link, so the view rests on policy direction rather than a fresh print. The most recent marker is from late February, when Reuters reported Chinese banks heeding a PBOC call to cut dollar deposit rates [[n1034]]. That is a push from the central bank, not evidence that borrowers are coming back. What would confirm the view is a loan figure in which household and corporate borrowing turns up for two months running. Until then, treat the factory rebound as a cyclical bounce rather than a credit upturn, and size China-linked positions to match.
Property

Prices are still falling, but more slowly. Reuters reported second-hand home price declines narrowing for a seventh straight month in February [[n1222]], while a Reuters poll expects home prices to drop further [[n0817]]. More distress is expected in Hong Kong property, where Winland is divesting assets [[n1287]], and hedge funds have started betting on a turnaround in the unloved sector [[n1039]]. A further month of narrowing declines would support the turnaround bets; a renewed fall in second-hand prices would undercut them.
Fiscal, Policy & Trade

Trade is the policy story, and it runs in both directions. Trump said the US will impose an additional 10% tariff on China [[n1166]]. China retaliated against US farm products [[n1313]], and CNBC reported counter-tariffs of up to 15% on some US goods from March 10 [[n1259]]. Domestic policy is opening rather than closing: China opened its telecoms sector to 13 foreign companies [[n1121]], and the Guardian reported the Two Sessions opening in Beijing as the world order roils [[n1309]]. A large new stimulus package is not the base case, so treat fiscal support as an option rather than a forecast.
Markets & Flows

Hong Kong is the strongest tape. The Hang Seng closed at 23,006.27, up 13.80% over 20 sessions though down 1.44% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). The mainland is lagging. The Shanghai Composite closed at 3,316.93 index points, up 1.98% over 20 sessions and down 1.66% over five. The CSI 300 tracker ASHR closed at 26.39 USD, down 0.68% in the prior session. KWEB, the China internet ETF, closed at 33.34 USD, up 6.59% over 20 sessions. The dollar-yuan rate rose 1.35% over 20 sessions to 7.2828, a weaker yuan (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Listings are drawing demand: Reuters reported Mixue jumping 47% on its Hong Kong debut as IPO volumes rebounded [[n5318]], and SCMP reported Chinese consumer stocks in demand as Mixue rides the IPO revival [[n1271]].
New / Most Important

Advanced chips are still reaching China. The Wall Street Journal reported Chinese buyers ordering Nvidia’s newest AI chips in defiance of US curbs [[n1227]], and Nikkei Asia reported Singapore suspecting Nvidia chips were smuggled via Malaysia [[n1302]]. This is the signal that matters because it ties the tech cycle to the export-control story, and both to the Hong Kong rally pulling the index higher. The consumer-tech side of the same story is visible too: Yahoo Finance reported Tencent’s AI bot passing DeepSeek as China’s favourite on iPhones [[n1305]].
Playbook ✓

Own Hong Kong internet and consumer names on confirmation. KWEB and the Hang Seng are the cleanest exposure, but buy them on pullbacks rather than chasing a 13.80% run over 20 sessions. Trim onshore A-share beta through ASHR if the counter-tariffs of March 10 [[n1259]] start to bite, and hedge the yuan leg, since dollar-yuan is up 1.35% over 20 sessions. The call changes if the official factory reading holds at a three-month high while loan data stay weak, because that combination means the rebound is an inventory story. ⚠ Divergence: the Hang Seng is up 13.80% over 20 sessions while Hong Kong’s January retail sales value fell 3.2% [[n1276]], so the market is pricing a consumer recovery the spending data have not yet shown.

geo.label: yen squeeze / tariff drag
parts: Macro Stance

Japan is absorbing the tariff shock through its corporate spending. Reuters reported Japanese corporate capex dropping for the first time in four years amid tariff fears [[n4334]], and the Bank of Japan chief warned of strong global uncertainty due to US tariffs [[n4246]]. Traders placed a record bet on a rising yen and further rate hikes [[n4350]]. The Japan Times wrote that Japanese stocks have stalled at 1989 levels as investors weigh tariffs and rates [[n2569]]. The macro read is weak demand with a firm currency, which is a poor mix for equities.
Activity & Currency

The yen is doing the work. USD/JPY closed at 150.7710, up 0.51% in the prior session but down 2.96% over 20 sessions, while the Nikkei 225 closed at 37,785.47, up 1.70% in the prior session and down 4.37% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Exporters carry the currency risk. Tokyo Electron fell 11.75% over 20 sessions to 22,380.00 JPY and Advantest fell 7.55% to 8,128.00 JPY, while Toyota rose 3.94% in the prior session to 2,795.00 JPY (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Households feel the cost side as well: The Japan Times reported consumers hunting for bargains as food inflation bites [[n2570]].
Playbook ✓

Stay underweight unhedged Japanese equities into the tariff start, and keep the yen as the funding-currency hedge that protects the book. Buy exporters only once the yen weakens. The trigger is USD/JPY back toward 155.3630, its 3 February level, which would restore the export tailwind. Until then, prefer domestic cyclicals with pricing power, and avoid adding to the semiconductor-equipment names that have fallen 11.75% and 7.55% over 20 sessions. The call changes if the Nikkei reclaims its 39,513.97 reference from 30 January with the yen still firm.

geo.label: easing tailwind / soft demand
parts: Macro Stance

A rate cut has ended the housing downturn. Reuters reported Australia’s housing market ending its downturn as the rate cut lifted sentiment [[n0273]]. The Reserve Bank’s own warning is the counterweight: weak incomes and high inflation if productivity lags [[n0241]]. AFR’s headline put it bluntly, that Chalmers has “damaged” RBA independence [[n0254]], which keeps the policy outlook noisy. The rate-cut tailwind is real but narrow, and the demand side is not yet strong enough to carry the equity market.
Demand & Financing

The Australian dollar closed at 0.6221 and the ASX 200 at 8,245.70 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). AUD/USD is down 2.35% over five sessions, while the index is down 1.60% over 20. Iron ore is the pressure point: it logged a monthly loss on China steel export concerns [[n0238]]. Financing is migrating: AFR reported global private credit funds set to storm Australia [[n5184]], and the banks are fighting over mortgage brokers, with CBA and NAB grappling with the rise of the broker channel [[n0253]]. BHP rose 1.43% in the prior session to 39.60 AUD.
Playbook ✓

Stay neutral on the ASX 200 and favour the banks only with a view on mortgage pricing. Keep iron-ore producers as a tactical trade rather than a core holding until China’s steel exports stabilise. The call turns constructive if AUD/USD reclaims its 0.6144 level from 3 February with the index holding its 8,379.40 reference from the same date. It turns defensive if the rate-cut sentiment fades and the housing rebound stalls.

geo.label: strong zloty / defence and banks
parts: Macro Stance

Poland is the one European market with a domestic turn. Bloomberg reported the zloty surging to a 10-year high against the dollar, fanned by a hawkish central bank [[n4430]]. A Polish manufacturing PMI signals a revival in industry and an end to almost three years of recession [[n4983]]. Wages keep rising: GUS published 2024 wage data showing Poles earning more [[n4986]]. Housing prices are rising more slowly than inflation, and developers are holding their per-square-metre prices [[n4952]]. Bankier reported the euro back up to 4.20 zloty [[n4971]], and Santander Bank warned that a strong zloty could weigh on GDP [[n4825]]. The zloty is strong, but the currency gain is not free: Business Insider Polska warned that a strong zloty is not only a benefit [[n4757]].
Markets

Poland’s proxies are up strongly. EPOL closed at 25.68 USD, up 8.68% over 20 sessions, and the WIG20TR tracker closed at 49.42 PLN, up 8.68% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). USD/PLN closed at 4.0048, down 2.73% over 20 sessions, and EUR/PLN at 4.1701, down 1.16%. Leadership is rotating toward energy and banks, and the spread is wide: Orlen closed at 64.12 PLN, up 21.05% over 20 sessions, against Allegro’s decline over the same window; mBank at 743.80 PLN, up 18.82%; PZU at 54.86 PLN, up 10.43%; and PKO Bank Polski at 69.92 PLN, up 6.33%. Consumer names are strong too: LPP at 18,210.00 PLN is up 13.67% and Dino Polska at 500.00 PLN is up 11.41%, while Allegro, at 28.09 PLN, is down 1.92% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Smaller names are moving too: JSW rose 12.03% over 20 sessions to 25.70 PLN, Asseco Poland rose 20.76% to 139.60 PLN, and CD Projekt rose 5.84% to 221.00 PLN (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Foreign money is in the bonds: Bankier reported more than ten central banks holding Polish treasuries [[n4976]], and Money.pl reported foreign central banks buying Polish treasuries as “big, strong players” [[n4985]].
Fiscal & Politics

The budget is the policy weak spot. Balcerowicz criticised spending that makes no sense under the current government [[n4849]]. The presidential race is tightening: POLITICO reported the nationalists sticking to Trump like glue ahead of the election [[n4440]], and an opinion poll suggests the pro-Kremlin candidate could enter the second round [[n4455]]. The president has vowed to spend 4.7% of GDP on defence this year [[n4370]], which is the fiscal anchor for the defence stocks. Governance is in the headlines as well: media reported a former Orlen board member detained by the CBA anti-corruption bureau [[n4961]], a story that sits awkwardly beside the dividend narrative.
Corporate & Sectors

Orlen is the anchor. Orlen and Equinor agreed to develop carbon capture projects [[n4456]], and Strefa Inwestorów reported that Orlen’s 2025 dividend could be the highest in its history [[n4789]]. Bank Pekao earned 6.4 billion zloty and wants to pay out half of it in dividends [[n4781]]. Dino is growing in a weak market and set a new all-time high [[n4858]]. Defence is the hottest theme in European equities, with shares setting fresh records [[n4987]]. Mining is less comfortable: a series of strong tremors hit two KGHM mines [[n4826]]. PGE GiEK’s chief says the Bełchatów site has all the advantages for a second nuclear plant [[n4953]]. PZU named Andrzej Klesyk as its new chief executive to lead Poland’s largest insurer [[n4810]].
Geopolitics & Security

The security backdrop is active. Poland scrambled military aircraft as Russian missiles targeted western Ukraine [[n4407]]. A report found Russia paid operatives to paint anti-government graffiti in Poland [[n4431]]. The Polish space agency is investigating a cyberattack on its systems [[n4458]], and Wałęsa said Trump’s treatment of Zelenskyy filled him with horror [[n4457]]. Polish equities trade the war as well: Ukrainian stocks surged on the Warsaw exchange on talk of a peace plan [[n4378]].
New / Most Important

The one signal that matters is the manufacturing turn meeting a strong currency. A PMI that signals revival [[n4983]], with the zloty at a 10-year high against the dollar [[n4430]], is the combination that lifts banks and domestic cyclicals while squeezing exporters.
Playbook ✓

Own the banks (PKO, Pekao, mBank) and Orlen on dividend visibility, and keep the defence names as a smaller satellite because their 20-session moves are extreme. Hedge the zloty leg with a modest EUR/PLN position, since a strong currency hurts exporters, and keep that hedge small so a currency reversal does not swamp the equity gain. The WIG20TR tracker at 49.42 PLN is the level to hold; a close back below its 45.47 PLN reference from 3 February would reopen the risk. ⚠ Divergence: a zloty at a 10-year high [[n4430]] against a manufacturing revival means exporters priced for a weak currency will lag the banks.
Narrative

The consensus still treats AI spending as the engine, but the leaders have turned. The technology ETF closed at 218.67 USD, down 3.04% in the prior session and 5.26% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Nvidia shares fell 9% on tariff fears, CNBC reported [[n2585]], and Forbes put it as Nvidia tanking as tariffs sink stocks [[n2579]]. Nvidia closed at 114.06 USD, down 8.69% in the prior session and 5.01% over 20 sessions from 120.07 USD on 31 January. The driver that matters now is the tariff overhang on the hardware cycle, not the demand story.
Reported

Dell reported a full-year EPS beat [[n0364]] and then lifted its dividend 18% alongside a $10 billion buyback [[n3264]]. Snowflake posted a big beat and the stock jumped, Barron’s reported [[n0355]]. Pure Storage beat on Q4 yet fell 12% in premarket trade, which Stocktwits framed as retail scrambling to buy the dip [[n5207]].
EPS Upside Watch

The set-up is in the hardware names that have been cut hardest. Nvidia’s guidance was optimistic but did not convince Wall Street [[n0358]], so the next print has to clear a bar the market already doubts. Dell’s buyback signals management confidence in cash generation, which makes its EPS path the cleaner set-up at 95.56 USD, down 7.76% over 20 sessions.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Beats are being sold. Pure Storage beat and still slid [[n5207]], and Nvidia’s 78% sales growth [[n0354]] did not stop the stock falling. Nvidia and Broadcom are testing chips on Intel’s manufacturing process, Reuters reported [[n2584]], a story about share moving between foundries rather than the AI pie growing.
Narrative

Platforms are split between advertising and AI optionality. The communication services ETF closed at 100.98 USD, down 1.00% in the prior session and 1.37% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Yahoo Finance laid out two reasons Meta broke its winning streak [[n5336]], while CNBC reported Meta planning a standalone AI app to compete with ChatGPT [[n5201]]. Alphabet fell 18.14% over 20 sessions to 167.01 USD.
Reported

Alphabet’s cost cuts are the most concrete corporate event in the sector: Google announced layoffs in its HR and cloud units as part of ongoing cost cuts [[n8153]]. Meta’s streak break is a share move rather than a reported result, so the sector’s reported side is thin and the narrative does the work.
EPS Upside Watch

Meta is set up on relative value, not on earnings. It closed at 655.05 USD, down 4.95% over 20 sessions, after the streak break [[n5336]]. The upside case is that the AI app adds engagement without adding cost, which is the question the next print has to answer. Netflix, at 973.70 USD and down 0.31% over 20 sessions, is the quieter defensive alternative.
⚡ Breaking Convention

The ad giants are no longer moving together. Alphabet is down 18.14% over 20 sessions while Meta is down 4.95%, so the sector is being sorted by company rather than traded as a block (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).
Narrative

Banks are being sold on the curve and on the tariff backdrop. The financials ETF closed at 51.74 USD, down 0.84% in the prior session but up 0.52% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Goldman Sachs warned that the S&P 500 rally may falter after a 5% selloff [[n8639]]. Goldman closed at 605.26 USD, down 5.49% over 20 sessions, and JPMorgan at 260.62 USD, down 2.50%.
Reported

BNY Mellon’s full-year 2024 revenue beat with EPS in line [[n2539]], and Goldman Sachs’ full-year 2024 results beat expectations [[n2562]]. The weak print was Ready Capital, whose shares plunged 28% after a Q4 loss and a dividend cut [[n2593]]. State Street agreed to buy Mizuho’s global custody business [[n2604]], a fee-franchise move rather than a balance-sheet one.
EPS Upside Watch

The upside is in custody and fee franchises, not in loan books. Regional lenders are the laggards: the regional-bank ETF KRE is down 4.64% over 20 sessions, so the sector needs evidence that funding costs are easing before the regional EPS lift is credible.
⚡ Breaking Convention

The big banks beat and still traded lower. BNY beat on revenue and Goldman beat [[n2539]] [[n2562]], yet Goldman is down 5.49% and Morgan Stanley down 6.72% over 20 sessions, so the sector is being priced on rates and tariffs rather than on the reported numbers.
Narrative

Oil is falling while gas is spiking. WTI closed at 68.37 USD, down 5.74% over 20 sessions, and Brent at 71.62 USD, down 6.70% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). The energy ETF closed at 87.82 USD, down 3.49% in the prior session. Henry Hub gas rose 35.41% over 20 sessions to 4.12 USD per MMBtu, and Reuters reported US natgas prices jumping 8% on record LNG flows [[n7201]].
Reported

The energy reporting in the window is thin, and the hard data point is gas. Reuters reported the jump on record LNG flows [[n7201]], and in the same news cycle Germany was reported not to be in talks to revive the Nord Stream 2 pipeline [[n2926]], which keeps the pipeline route closed for now.
EPS Upside Watch

The set-up is gas, not crude. Producers with gas exposure are the names that gain if the LNG flows hold. Exxon closed at 107.76 USD, up 0.87% over 20 sessions, and Chevron at 153.09 USD, up 2.61%, while ConocoPhillips, at 92.63 USD, is down 6.27% and is the most crude-exposed of the three.

The usual oil-and-gas pairing has broken. Gas is up 35.41% over 20 sessions while crude is down 5.74%, and the energy ETF is only up 0.21% over the same window, which says the market is not paying for the gas move in the majors (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).
Narrative

Factories are holding while the tariffs threaten the supply chain. The ISM manufacturing index printed 50.3 for February [[n8278]], but TradingView reported the slowdown coming in more than expected [[n8301]], and price pressures surged ahead of the tariffs [[n1315]]. The industrials ETF closed at 134.39 USD, down 1.42% in the prior session and 2.86% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).
Reported

Rolls-Royce upgraded its forecasts and its shares soared more than 18%, Investing.com reported [[n5214]]. The Caterpillar line is weaker: it is down 10.61% over 20 sessions to 332.04 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).
EPS Upside Watch

Rolls-Royce has shown the template: a guidance upgrade is rewarded even in a soft industrial tape. The next industrials with a cash-flow guide are the set-up. Airbus, at 174.38 EUR, rose 5.24% in the prior session and 4.68% over 20 sessions, so the European aerospace leg has momentum going into any print.
⚡ Breaking Convention

The manufacturing data are holding up better than the stock tape. An ISM reading of 50.3 [[n8278]] sits beside an ETF down 2.86% over 20 sessions, which says the market is discounting tariffs, not the current factory activity.
Narrative

Consumer discretionary is where the damage shows. The sector ETF closed at 211.98 USD, down 1.84% in the prior session and 8.70% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Tesla is the largest single reason. Morgan Stanley reinstated it as a top pick with a $430 target [[n5369]], but the stock is down 29.65% over 20 sessions. Target fell 12.44% over 20 sessions to 120.76 USD, and Lululemon fell 16.03% to 347.81 USD.
Reported

Tesla sales almost halved in Europe last month and were surpassed by a Chinese rival, Business Insider reported [[n5657]]. Reuters reported Tesla’s market value tumbling below $1 trillion as its Europe sales slumped [[n5659]]. Those are the reported facts the bulls have to argue around.
EPS Upside Watch

The next consumer print is the test, and the bar is low. Target and Lululemon have already been cut hard over 20 sessions, so a guidance hold would be enough to lift the group. Warren Buffett said tariffs leave consumers footing the bill [[n8660]], which keeps the discretionary bar high on pricing.
⚡ Breaking Convention
The habit this cuts against is buying the Tesla dip. Musk’s claim that Tesla’s profit could grow tenfold over five years [[n2556]] runs against a sales slump in the cars that define the sector.
Narrative

Staples are quietly working. The staples ETF closed at 83.52 USD, up 0.53% in the prior session and 5.75% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Coca-Cola rose 13.93% over 20 sessions to 72.32 USD, and Costco rose 6.83% to 1,046.85 USD. The defensive bid is real, and it is not a sign of a consumer boom.
Reported

Kroger, a Buffett pick, paid investors, 24/7 Wall St. reported [[n3156]]. The concrete corporate news is pricing: Walmart rose 4.18% over five sessions to 97.59 USD, and Procter & Gamble rose 5.78% over 20 sessions to 175.59 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).
EPS Upside Watch

Pricing power is the upside case. Staples can hold margins if they pass tariff costs on, but Buffett’s point that consumers pay the tariff bill [[n8660]] puts a limit on how far that goes. Walmart and Costco are the names with the strongest set-up on that test.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Staples rise while discretionary falls, which is the defensive rotation in plain sight. The convention that a risk-off tape lifts only gold and utilities is breaking, because the staples are doing the work (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).
Narrative

Health care is the defensive with a story. The sector ETF closed at 149.58 USD, up 1.85% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Eli Lilly rose 14.63% over 20 sessions to 929.72 USD, and Bank of America raised its Madrigal target to $239 from $154 [[n3181]]. The sector is being bought for growth as well as for safety.
Reported

Hims & Hers plunged 22% on concerns over its weight-loss business and margins [[n5019]], and Reuters reported looming curbs on drug compounding clouding the forecast [[n5020]]. Hims & Hers’ full-year 2024 results came in line with expectations [[n5099]].
EPS Upside Watch

Lilly is the momentum name, and its upside is in the next print rather than the price. Madrigal’s target raise [[n3181]] is the analyst set-up, with the upside resting on the next print rather than on the stock’s recent move.
⚡ Breaking Convention

The managed-care half of health care is not working. UnitedHealth is down 13.91% over 20 sessions to 467.05 USD while the sector ETF is up 1.85%, so the sector average hides a split between drug names and insurers.
Narrative

Materials are split between copper and steel. The materials ETF closed at 86.98 USD, down 2.01% in the prior session and 2.04% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Iron ore logged a monthly loss on China steel export concerns [[n0238]]. Copper is the asset here, not a China growth gauge: it closed at 4.58 USD per pound, up 7.38% over 20 sessions, on the AI data-centre and grid build-out.
Reported
Freeport-McMoRan closed at 35.53 USD, down 0.89% over 20 sessions, and Alcoa at 31.33 USD, down 11.30%. Money.pl argued that Europe must invest in mining to build a copper future [[n4876]].

Copper miners are the set-up, and their earnings upside rides the metal. Freeport’s 35.53 USD close is the level that matters, since it has barely moved while copper has risen 7.38% over 20 sessions.

Copper is up 7.38% over 20 sessions while the materials ETF is down 2.04%. The metal is rising while the sector falls, the reverse of the usual China-growth read, which is why copper gets treated as an asset here.

Rates relief is reaching real estate. The real-estate ETF closed at 43.52 USD, up 2.59% over five sessions and 5.07% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03). Mortgage rates fell: Yahoo Finance reported rates dropping by 28 basis points in February [[n8233]], and on 28 February it reported the lowest mortgage rates of the year [[n8209]].

Housing volume has not followed the rates. Bloomberg reported US pending home sales falling to a record low on weather and rates [[n8186]], which is the sector’s reported side and it is weak.
EPS Upside Watch

Housing-linked REITs are the set-up if mortgage rates stay low. The sector has to show volume, not just rate relief, before an earnings lift is credible. The ETF’s 5.07% gain over 20 sessions is ahead of that proof.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Pending home sales hit a record low [[n8186]] while the real-estate ETF rose 5.07% over 20 sessions. The rally is a rate bet rather than a volume bet, and the sector is pricing a recovery the transactions have not yet shown.

Power names are having an AI hangover. The utilities ETF closed at 79.33 USD, up 1.86% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03), but Vistra fell 26.23% over 20 sessions and Constellation Energy fell 22.56%. Vistra’s full-year 2024 results were strong on paper, with EPS of US$7.28 against US$3.63 in 2023 [[n2506]]. The stock has not followed, which says the market is pricing the next contract rather than the last year’s earnings.
EPS Upside Watch

The upside is a contract, not a quarter. Vistra’s data-centre deal is the thing investors are still waiting for [[n5308]], so the EPS set-up is conditional on a signed agreement rather than on the reported year.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Defensive utilities are working while the AI-power growth names are not. Duke rose 5.96% over 20 sessions and Southern Company rose 8.22%, while Vistra is down 26.23%. Stocktwits reported Vistra’s rally ahead of Q4 earnings drawing a retail bearish read [[n5233]], which shows the crowd doubting the AI-power premium.

Ford pulled back on stocking EVs at regional hubs instead of dealer lots, Automotive News reported [[n5182]]. Valeo and Forvia said they will pass tariff costs on to customers [[n1175]]. French new-car registrations fell on lower Stellantis sales [[n2889]].

Volkswagen and BMW are the set-up if tariff pass-through holds, and Valeo and Forvia have said they will pass the costs on [[n1175]]. The upside is in pricing rather than volume, which is why the premium names are the ones carrying the sector.
⚡ Breaking Convention

The sector is not moving as one. Volkswagen is up 12.58% over 20 sessions while Stellantis, at 12.34 USD, is down 6.02%, so the ETF average hides a split between the premium names and the volume names.

Semis are the sector that is breaking. The chip ETF closed at 201.15 USD, down 3.53% in the prior session and 7.78% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-03).
